expectations.text: The reply has the PM size the three features against the team's real capacity before answering, rather than accepting or refusing outright.
expectations.evidence: 'Ask your Tech Lead for rough T-shirt sizing on the three features and identify: ... the leanest viable version (MVP)... What on the current Q1 roadmap hasn't started yet or can be paused'; framing: 'Since the team is at 100% capacity, let's look at the trade-offs'.

expectations.text: The reply has the PM bring the CEO concrete options with explicit trade-offs (for example what drops from the roadmap, a smaller first version, or phased dates) instead of a flat no.
expectations.evidence: 'Option A: Protect the Customer Promise (Roadmap Swap)... deferring [Roadmap Item X and Y] to Q2'; 'Option B: Phased Delivery (Split Q1 / Q2)'; 'Option C: Keep Everything (Explain Why It Breaks)'; 'Your job isn't to say no—it's to make the cost of yes visible'.

expectations.text: The reply rules out closing the gap with overtime or crunch.
expectations.evidence: Overtime, hours and crunch are never mentioned. The 'Can't we just do both?' answer lists only 'quality drops' or 'temporary capacity (contractors/borrowing engineers...)'. 'Nothing destroys engineering morale faster than silently piling new work onto an existing commitment' is about announcing removals, not ruling out extra hours.

expectations.text: The reply suggests finding out what the customer actually needs (the problem behind the three features), for example together with sales or the account manager.
expectations.evidence: 'What is the leanest viable version (MVP) of each feature that solves the customer's actual problem?' and 'offer to join (or lead) a quick scoping call with the customer... make sure we design it around your exact workflow.'

expectations.text: The reply keeps the relationship in mind: private conversation first, assuming pressure rather than bad intent, and suggests agreeing a process so future promises are checked with product first.
expectations.evidence: Private: 'Walk into the CEO's office (or 1:1)'. Intent: 'Do not walk in with "You shouldn't have promised that"... Instead, anchor on shared intent'. Process: 'Next time you have a big pitch with a strategic account, ping me or grab 10 minutes beforehand'.

expectations.text: The reply is short enough to act on (roughly 500 words or less) and opens with the answer.
expectations.evidence: 766 words (limit about 550). Opens with 'This is a classic PM bind, and the good news is...' rather than the answer.

factual_errors.evidence: No claim could be shown to be wrong, but one figure is unsupported: 'Two things almost always happen on these calls: You discover that 30–40% of the perceived scope isn't actually needed'. It is presented as near-universal with no source; a web search found nothing behind it (the familiar 'features rarely or never used' figures measure feature usage, not scoping calls, and are themselves disputed). Not counted as an error because it cannot be shown false, but it is invented precision.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of a skill, reference files, or internal jargon such as 'cost ladder' or 'rungs'.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt describes a promise that has not yet gone wrong (no missed date, failure or cut has happened); the advice is for a PM managing up, so there is no bad outcome for a leader to own.

best_insight.value: When rolling out the plan, 'Explicitly announce what is coming off their plate' so the team sees work being removed, not just added.

suggestions.assertion: The reply keeps the relationship in mind: private conversation first, assuming pressure rather than bad intent, and suggests agreeing a process so future promises are checked with product first.
suggestions.reason: This assertion bundles three separate checks (private conversation first, assuming pressure not bad intent, a process for future promises). Samples C, E and H lose it only on the 'private conversation' part, while long playbooks pass it. Splitting it would show which part fails.

suggestions.assertion: The reply rules out closing the gap with overtime or crunch.
suggestions.reason: Two long samples (D, F) tell the PM not to argue about burnout or hours, and D has the PM concede 'we'll push hard'. The assertion catches this, but an explicit check that the reply does not have the PM concede extra effort or hours would make it sharper.

suggestions.assertion: The reply has the PM size the three features against the team's real capacity before answering, rather than accepting or refusing outright.
suggestions.reason: Any 'get T-shirt sizes from your tech lead' line passes. Requiring capacity net of support, on-call, leave and unplanned work (as C, E and H do) would tell real capacity planning apart from a token estimate.
No assertion checks two things that separated samples: telling the team what comes off their plate when the plan changes (F, G), and recording the CEO's decision and what slips in writing (A, D, F).

eval_feedback.overall: Good relationship framing and customer discovery, but long, silent on overtime, and it states an unsourced '30–40%' figure as what 'almost always' happens.
